title: D2.2 Gene expression
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: D2.2 Gene expression — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic D2.2.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering D2.2 Gene expression, guide topic D2.2.
final_note: You worked through D2.2 Gene expression — 11 guide statements.

concepts.def: The mechanism by which the information in a gene has an effect on the phenotype of a cell or organism. Its most common stages are transcription of the gene to produce mRNA, translation of the mRNA to produce a polypeptide, and the function of the resulting protein product, such as an enzyme catalysing a reaction. A gene that is present in a cell but not transcribed is not being expressed.

The observable characteristics of a cell or organism, including structures, metabolic activities and behaviour. Genes affect the phenotype indirectly: the direct product of expressing a gene is a protein, and it is the functioning of that protein, together with environmental influences, that produces the characteristic.

The third stage of gene expression, in which the polypeptide made by translation carries out its role in the cell. Many gene products are enzymes, so the characteristic controlled by the gene is often the product of a reaction the enzyme catalyses rather than the protein itself; for example, the enzyme tyrosinase catalyses a step in the synthesis of the pigment melanin.

A specific base sequence in DNA, located near the start of a gene and upstream of it, to which transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind so that transcription of the gene can be initiated. The promoter is a control sequence: it is not part of the sequence that is transcribed into mRNA and it does not code for part of the polypeptide.

A specific base sequence in DNA to which activator transcription factors bind, increasing the rate of transcription of a gene. An enhancer may be thousands of base pairs away from the gene it regulates, upstream or downstream of it; looping of the DNA brings the proteins bound at the enhancer into contact with those bound at the promoter.

A protein that binds to a specific base sequence in DNA, such as a promoter or an enhancer, and regulates transcription of a gene. In eukaryotic cells, transcription factors must bind to the promoter before RNA polymerase can bind and begin transcription; other transcription factors increase or decrease the rate of transcription, so which transcription factors are present and active in a cell helps to determine which genes are expressed.

The breakdown of mRNA molecules in the cytoplasm by nuclease enzymes, which hydrolyse the RNA into nucleotides. Because a molecule of mRNA can be translated repeatedly for as long as it persists, controlling how quickly it is degraded regulates how much polypeptide is made from a gene. In human cells, an mRNA may persist for anything from minutes up to days before it is broken down.

An enzyme that hydrolyses the phosphodiester bonds of a nucleic acid. The nucleases that degrade mRNA in the cytoplasm end the translation of that mRNA; they do not affect the gene in the nucleus, which can be transcribed again.

The development of patterns of differentiation in the cells of a multicellular organism. All the body cells develop from a single zygote and contain the same genome; they become different from each other because different genes are expressed in different cells, not because their DNA base sequences differ.

A change in the pattern of gene expression of a cell that does not involve any change to the base sequence of its DNA. Epigenetic changes therefore alter the phenotype of the cell but not its genotype, which distinguishes them from mutations.

All of the genetic information of a cell or organism: the complete DNA base sequence, including every gene and the non-coding sequences. Apart from rare mutations, every body cell of a multicellular organism has the same genome, and it does not change as the cell differentiates or as conditions change.

All of the RNA molecules, including mRNA, that are present in a cell at a particular time. Because no cell expresses all of its genes, the transcriptome contains transcripts of only part of the genome; it differs between cell types and changes as a cell responds to its conditions.

All of the proteins present in a cell at a particular time. The proteome differs between cell types and changes over time, and it does not simply mirror the transcriptome: the amount of each protein also depends on how rapidly its mRNA is translated and degraded and on how long the protein itself persists.

A chemical group added to DNA or to the histone proteins of a nucleosome that alters gene expression without altering the DNA base sequence. Methylation of cytosine in a promoter and methylation of amino acids in histones are examples.

The addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases in the DNA of a gene's promoter. This represses transcription and therefore the expression of the gene downstream of the promoter. The methylated cytosine is still cytosine and still pairs with guanine, so the base sequence is unchanged.

The addition of methyl groups to amino acids in the histone proteins around which DNA is wound in nucleosomes. Depending on which amino acids are methylated, this can cause transcription of the associated genes to be repressed or activated; the details of how this is achieved are not required.

The passing on of a change in gene expression, and so of a phenotypic change, to daughter cells or to offspring without any change in the nucleotide sequence of the DNA. It is possible when epigenetic tags such as DNA methylation or histone modification remain in place during mitosis (giving daughter cells the same pattern of expression) or during meiosis (so that the tags are present in gametes).

A change in which genes a cell or organism expresses, caused by a factor in its surroundings rather than by a change in its genes. Such factors often act by altering epigenetic tags, so the pattern of expression, and therefore the phenotype, changes while the genotype stays the same.

The example named in the guide: studies of people exposed to air pollution, such as particulate matter from traffic, have found altered patterns of methyl tags on the DNA of their cells, including on genes involved in inflammation and immune responses. The DNA base sequence is not changed by the pollution; its effect is on gene expression.

concepts.term: Removal of epigenetic tags from gametes
concepts.def: During the formation of sperm and ova and in the early embryo, most of the epigenetic tags carried on the DNA and histones are removed. This allows the cells of the embryo to develop a fresh pattern of differentiation. Some tags are not removed, so a few genes carry different tags depending on whether they came from the sperm or the ovum, and are expressed differently according to the parent that supplied them.

Lion–tiger hybrids. A liger has a lion father and a tiger mother and grows much larger than either parent species; a tigon has a tiger father and a lion mother and does not. Both receive one set of lion chromosomes and one set of tiger chromosomes, so the size difference is not due to different genes. It arises because tags that were not removed from the sperm and ovum cause growth-related genes to be expressed differently depending on which parent supplied them.

An investigation that compares monozygotic (identical) twins, who developed from one zygote and so have the same genome. Because their genes are the same, differences in gene expression or phenotype between the twins must be due to differences in their environment, so such studies are used to investigate the effects of the environment on gene expression, for example by comparing the patterns of DNA methylation in twins of different ages or with different lifestyles.

A group of genes in the bacterium Escherichia coli, transcribed together as one unit, that code for the proteins needed to take up and break down lactose, including the enzyme beta-galactosidase. Transcription is controlled by a repressor protein binding to the operator, a base sequence next to the promoter. The lactose-metabolizing genes are expressed only when lactose is present.

A protein that binds to a specific base sequence in DNA and prevents transcription. The lac repressor binds to the operator of the lac operon, blocking RNA polymerase, when lactose is absent. When lactose is present, lactose (as its isomer allolactose) binds to the repressor and changes its shape so that it can no longer bind to the operator, allowing the genes to be transcribed.

The example of estrogen: a steroid hormone that passes through the plasma membrane of a target cell and binds to a receptor protein inside the cell. The hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, binding to specific base sequences in DNA and altering the transcription of target genes, so the hormone changes the pattern of gene expression in the cell.

mcqs.q: A gene affects the colour of a flower's petals. Which sequence of stages is the mechanism by which the information in this gene has its effect on the phenotype?
options: Transcription of the gene to mRNA, translation of the mRNA to a protein, then the function of that protein
Direct action of the base sequence of the gene on the petal cells, without any protein product
Transcription and translation of the gene to make the pigment molecule that colours the petal
Replication of the gene in every petal cell, so that copies of the gene produce the pigment
mcqs.specStatementText: How a gene reaches the phenotype: transcription, translation, protein at work
mcqs.explain: These are the most common stages of gene expression. The protein product, often an enzyme, is what acts on the phenotype: here it could be an enzyme catalysing a step in pigment synthesis.
rationales: These are the most common stages of gene expression. The protein product, often an enzyme, is what acts on the phenotype: here it could be an enzyme catalysing a step in pigment synthesis.

A student who reads 'a gene for petal colour' literally picks this. DNA does not act on the phenotype directly; information in the gene has its effect through the protein made when the gene is expressed.

A student who thinks the product of a gene is the characteristic itself picks this. Translation produces a polypeptide, not a pigment; the pigment is made by the function of the protein, for example an enzyme catalysing its synthesis.
A student who confuses copying DNA with expressing it picks this. Replication copies the genome for cell division; expression begins with transcription of the gene into mRNA.

mcqs.q: In humans, a gene codes for the enzyme tyrosinase, which catalyses a step in the synthesis of the pigment melanin. A person with two non-functional alleles of this gene has albinism. What is the direct product of expressing this gene?
options: The pigment melanin, which the gene codes for
The enzyme tyrosinase, made by translation
The skin colour that the gene determines
More copies of the gene in each skin cell
mcqs.specStatementText: How a gene reaches the phenotype: transcription, translation, protein at work
mcqs.explain: The direct product of gene expression is the polypeptide made by translation of the gene's mRNA: here the enzyme tyrosinase. Its function, catalysing a step in melanin synthesis, is what affects the phenotype.
rationales: A student who treats the characteristic as the gene product picks this. Melanin is not a protein and is not coded for by any gene; it is produced by the function of the enzyme that the gene codes for.

The direct product of gene expression is the polypeptide made by translation of the gene's mRNA: here the enzyme tyrosinase. Its function, catalysing a step in melanin synthesis, is what affects the phenotype.
A student who thinks genes act directly on the phenotype picks this. Skin colour is the eventual effect; it is reached only through transcription, translation and the function of the enzyme.
A student who confuses replication with expression picks this. Expressing a gene does not make more copies of it; it makes mRNA and then a polypeptide.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the promoter of a gene in a eukaryotic cell?
options: The first part of the gene to be transcribed, which codes for the first amino acids of the polypeptide
A protein that binds to an enhancer sequence and increases the rate of transcription of the gene
A sequence near the start of the gene to which transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind
A base sequence that RNA polymerase binds to by itself, with no other proteins required
mcqs.specStatementText: Proteins bind promoters and enhancers to control transcription
mcqs.explain: The promoter is a specific base sequence in DNA. Transcription factors bind to it first, and this allows RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription of the gene downstream.
rationales: A student who pictures the gene as one continuous piece of code picks this. The promoter lies upstream of the transcribed region and is not copied into mRNA, so it codes for nothing.
A student who thinks promoters are proteins picks this. The promoter is a DNA sequence; the proteins that bind to enhancers and promoters are transcription factors.
The promoter is a specific base sequence in DNA. Transcription factors bind to it first, and this allows RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription of the gene downstream.
A student who learned transcription as 'RNA polymerase binds and copies' picks this. In eukaryotic cells transcription factors must bind to the promoter before RNA polymerase can attach.

mcqs.q: In a eukaryotic cell, a non-coding base sequence located 20 000 base pairs upstream of a gene is deleted. The promoter of the gene is intact, but transcription of the gene falls to a much lower rate. What is the best explanation?
options: The deleted sequence coded for a transcription factor, so less is now made
The deletion is unrelated, because a sequence so far away cannot affect the gene
The deleted sequence was part of the transcribed region, so a shorter mRNA is made
The deleted sequence was an enhancer to which activator proteins bound
mcqs.specStatementText: Proteins bind promoters and enhancers to control transcription
mcqs.explain: Enhancers can lie thousands of base pairs from the gene they regulate. Transcription factors bound to the enhancer increase the rate of transcription, so deleting it lowers the rate even though the promoter is intact.
rationales: A student who confuses the DNA sequence with the protein that binds it picks this. The stem states that the sequence was non-coding; an enhancer is a binding site for transcription factors, not a gene for one.

A student who judges influence by distance along the DNA picks this. Looping of the DNA brings proteins bound at a distant enhancer into contact with those at the promoter, so distant sequences do regulate transcription.

A student who thinks control sequences upstream of a gene are transcribed along with it picks this. Transcription begins downstream of the promoter, so a non-coding sequence 20 000 base pairs upstream is never copied into mRNA; it is a control sequence (an enhancer) whose loss reduces the rate of transcription, not the length of the transcript.

Enhancers can lie thousands of base pairs from the gene they regulate. Transcription factors bound to the enhancer increase the rate of transcription, so deleting it lowers the rate even though the promoter is intact.

mcqs.q: Two genes in a human cell are transcribed at the same rate. mRNA from gene P is broken down by nucleases about 10 minutes after it is made; mRNA from gene Q persists for about two days. Assume both mRNAs are translated at the same rate while they persist. Which statement is correct?
options: More protein is made from gene Q, because each of its mRNA molecules is translated many times before degradation
The amount of protein made from each gene is the same, because their rates of transcription are equal
More protein is made from gene P, because its mRNA is used up and replaced much more rapidly
The amount of protein from gene Q can be changed more quickly if its rate of transcription changes
mcqs.specStatementText: How long an mRNA lasts controls how much protein is made
mcqs.explain: An mRNA can be translated repeatedly for as long as it persists. With equal transcription, the long-lived mRNA of gene Q yields many more polypeptides, which is why control of mRNA degradation regulates translation.
rationales: An mRNA can be translated repeatedly for as long as it persists. With equal transcription, the long-lived mRNA of gene Q yields many more polypeptides, which is why control of mRNA degradation regulates translation.

A student who thinks transcription rate alone sets the amount of protein picks this. Each mRNA from gene Q is translated for days, each from gene P for minutes, so far more protein is made from gene Q.
A student who thinks each mRNA delivers one message and is destroyed picks this. Faster turnover means each mRNA is translated fewer times, not that more protein is made.
A student who equates a stable mRNA with a better one picks this. Gene Q's mRNA keeps being translated for days after transcription changes, so it is gene P whose protein level can change quickly.

mcqs.q: Which statement about epigenesis, the development of patterns of differentiation in a multicellular organism, is correct?
options: Cells become different from each other because each type keeps only the genes it needs
Cells become different from each other through changes in gene expression, not in DNA sequence
Cells become different from each other through mutations that alter the sequences of their genes
Cells become different from each other by expressing all of their genes at different rates
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells differentiate by expressing different genes, not by changing DNA
mcqs.explain: All the cells derive from one zygote and share a genome. Patterns of differentiation develop as different genes are switched on and off in different cells; the base sequences are not altered, so phenotype but not genotype changes.
rationales: A student who thinks differentiated cells discard unused genes picks this. Every body cell retains the complete genome; differentiation changes which genes are expressed, not which are present.

All the cells derive from one zygote and share a genome. Patterns of differentiation develop as different genes are switched on and off in different cells; the base sequences are not altered, so phenotype but not genotype changes.
A student who treats any developmental change in DNA activity as a mutation picks this. Epigenetic changes leave the base sequence unaltered, so genotype is unchanged while phenotype changes.
A student who assumes every gene is in use in every cell picks this. No cell expresses all of its genes; many genes are not transcribed at all in a given cell type.

mcqs.q: A liver cell and a neuron from the same person are compared. Which comparison is correct?
options: They have different genomes, because each has kept different genes
They have the same transcriptome, because both cells transcribe all of their genes
They have the same genome but different transcriptomes and proteomes
They have the same proteome, because the same genes code for the same proteins
mcqs.specStatementText: Genome, transcriptome and proteome are not the same list
mcqs.explain: The genome is the same in all body cells. The two cells express different sets of genes, so the RNA present (transcriptome) and the proteins present (proteome) differ, and this is what makes them differentiated.
rationales: A student who thinks differentiation removes genes picks this. Both cells developed from the same zygote by mitosis and contain the same genome.
A student who assumes all genes are expressed everywhere picks this. No cell expresses all of its genes, and the two cell types transcribe different subsets, so their transcriptomes differ.

The genome is the same in all body cells. The two cells express different sets of genes, so the RNA present (transcriptome) and the proteins present (proteome) differ, and this is what makes them differentiated.

A student who reads the proteome straight off the gene list picks this. Having the same genes does not mean making the same proteins; the proteome reflects which genes are expressed, which differs between the cells.

mcqs.q: In a study of one type of human cell, about 20 000 protein-coding genes were identified in the genome. mRNA from about 11 000 of these genes was detected in the cell, and the amount of each protein present correlated only weakly with the amount of its mRNA. What is the best conclusion?
options: The cell has lost the 9 000 genes for which no mRNA could be detected in the study
The weak correlation must be an error, because each mRNA gives the same amount of protein
The transcriptome is fixed, so the 9 000 silent genes cannot be expressed in this cell later
The cell transcribes only some of its genes, and protein amounts are also regulated after transcription
mcqs.specStatementText: Genome, transcriptome and proteome are not the same list
mcqs.explain: Transcripts from only 11 000 of 20 000 genes show that the cell does not express all of its genes. The weak correlation shows that the proteome is not a copy of the transcriptome: translation rate, mRNA degradation and protein turnover also set protein amounts.
rationales: A student who thinks unused genes are discarded picks this. The genes were identified in the cell's genome; they are present but not transcribed in this cell type.
A student who extends one gene–one polypeptide to quantities picks this. mRNAs differ in how often they are translated and how quickly they are degraded, so a weak correlation is expected.
A student who treats the transcriptome as a fixed property picks this. The transcriptome is a snapshot; genes that are silent now can be switched on if conditions or signals change.

Transcripts from only 11 000 of 20 000 genes show that the cell does not express all of its genes. The weak correlation shows that the proteome is not a copy of the transcriptome: translation rate, mRNA degradation and protein turnover also set protein amounts.

mcqs.q: Cytosine bases in the DNA of a gene's promoter become methylated. What is the effect on the gene?
options: Transcription of the gene downstream is repressed, so it is not expressed
Translation of the gene's mRNA is blocked, because ribosomes cannot read methylated codons
The base sequence of the gene is altered, so a different polypeptide is produced from it
Transcription of the gene is increased, because the methyl tag marks it for expression
mcqs.specStatementText: Methyl tags on promoters and histones
mcqs.explain: Methylation of cytosine in a promoter is an epigenetic tag that represses transcription and therefore the expression of the gene downstream, without any change in the base sequence.
rationales: Methylation of cytosine in a promoter is an epigenetic tag that represses transcription and therefore the expression of the gene downstream, without any change in the base sequence.
A student who pictures methyl groups as obstacles on the message picks this. The tag is on the DNA of the promoter and acts at transcription, so no mRNA is made in the first place.
A student who thinks methylation is a mutation picks this. A methylated cytosine is still cytosine and still pairs with guanine; the sequence, and so the genotype, is unchanged.
A student who takes a tag to be a label for use picks this. Methylation of the promoter has the opposite effect: it switches transcription of the gene off.

mcqs.q: In a study, methylation of one particular amino acid in a histone was found in the nucleosomes of genes that were being actively transcribed, while methylation of a different amino acid in the same histone was found in the nucleosomes of genes that were silenced. What does this show?
options: The finding on active genes must be an error, because methylation only ever represses transcription
Methylation of histones can either activate or repress transcription, depending on the tag
The methyl groups must be on the DNA wound around the histones, because histones are not modified
Methylation of histones activates transcription, so the silenced genes were switched off by another tag
mcqs.specStatementText: Methyl tags on promoters and histones
mcqs.explain: Methyl groups on different amino acids of a histone are different epigenetic tags, and the guide states that histone methylation can cause transcription to be repressed or activated. The details of how this is achieved are not required.
rationales: A student who has learned methylation as a single off switch picks this. That rule holds for cytosine in a promoter, but methylation of amino acids in histones can repress or activate transcription.

Methyl groups on different amino acids of a histone are different epigenetic tags, and the guide states that histone methylation can cause transcription to be repressed or activated. The details of how this is achieved are not required.
A student who merges histone methylation with DNA methylation picks this. Histones are proteins, and the tags described are on their amino acids, not on DNA bases.
A student who thinks tags label genes for use picks this. The data show histone methylation on silenced genes as well as active ones, so histone methylation can repress as well as activate.

mcqs.q: In a skin cell, the promoter of gene G is methylated and the gene is not expressed. The cell divides by mitosis. What is the most likely state of gene G in the daughter cells, and why?
options: Expressed, because epigenetic tags are lost whenever DNA is replicated
Not expressed, because the methylation has changed the base sequence of the gene
Not expressed, because the methyl tags remained in place through mitosis
Not expressed in the person's children, because the tags pass to offspring
mcqs.specStatementText: Expression patterns can be inherited if tags stay in place
mcqs.explain: Epigenetic tags such as promoter methylation can remain in place during mitosis, so the daughter cells inherit the same pattern of gene expression. The base sequence of gene G is unchanged; this is epigenetic inheritance.
rationales: A student who thinks only the base sequence survives cell division picks this. Methylation patterns can be maintained through mitosis, which is how differentiated cells produce daughter cells of the same type.
A student who treats methylation as a mutation picks this. The daughter cells do inherit the silenced state, but the base sequence of gene G is not altered; only the tag is passed on.

Epigenetic tags such as promoter methylation can remain in place during mitosis, so the daughter cells inherit the same pattern of gene expression. The base sequence of gene G is unchanged; this is epigenetic inheritance.

A student who thinks acquired epigenetic changes go to the next generation picks this. A tag in a skin cell is passed only to that cell's daughter cells; reaching offspring would require the tag to be in a gamete.

mcqs.q: Blood cells from people living in a city with high levels of particulate air pollution were compared with blood cells from people living in an area with clean air. The pattern of methyl tags on the DNA of several genes differed between the two groups, but the base sequences of those genes were the same. Which conclusion is best supported by these findings?
options: Air pollution acted as a mutagen, changing the genes in the blood cells
The two groups must have differed genetically before any exposure to pollution
The altered tags will be inherited by the children of the exposed people
Air pollution altered gene expression without altering genotype
mcqs.specStatementText: The environment changes which genes are expressed
mcqs.explain: Altered methyl tags with an unchanged base sequence is exactly an environmental effect on gene expression: the pattern of expression, and so the phenotype of the cells, changed while the genotype did not.
rationales: A student whose only model of environmental action on DNA is mutation picks this. The base sequences were the same in both groups, so the genes were not mutated; what differed was the epigenetic tags.
A student who believes gene activity is fixed from conception picks this. The base sequences examined were the same in both groups; the difference lay in tags that the environment can alter.

A student who assumes acquired epigenetic changes pass to offspring picks this. The tags were observed in blood cells; nothing in the study shows that they are present in gametes or survive to the next generation.

Altered methyl tags with an unchanged base sequence is exactly an environmental effect on gene expression: the pattern of expression, and so the phenotype of the cells, changed while the genotype did not.

mcqs.q: Female honeybee larvae in a hive are genetically alike. Larvae fed only on royal jelly develop into fertile queens; larvae switched to a diet of worker jelly develop into smaller, sterile workers. Which explanation is consistent with the understanding of gene expression?
options: The diet alters epigenetic tags, so the two castes express different sets of the same genes
Larvae fed worker jelly lose the genes that are needed for queen development
Royal jelly contains a mutagen that alters the base sequence of the larva's growth genes
The diet cannot cause the difference, so the caste of each larva must be fixed at fertilization
mcqs.specStatementText: The environment changes which genes are expressed
mcqs.explain: This is an environmental effect on gene expression: the food a larva receives changes tags such as DNA methylation, altering which genes are switched on, so genetically alike larvae develop different phenotypes.
rationales: This is an environmental effect on gene expression: the food a larva receives changes tags such as DNA methylation, altering which genes are switched on, so genetically alike larvae develop different phenotypes.
A student who thinks unused genes are discarded picks this. Workers keep the whole genome; the genes for queen development are present but not expressed.

A student whose only model for an environmental effect is mutation picks this. Diet acts on gene expression through epigenetic tags; the DNA sequence of a queen is the same as that of her worker sisters.

A student who thinks gene activity is set at conception picks this. The larvae are genetically alike and the stem states that the caste depends on the diet given, so the environment must be acting on gene expression.

mcqs.q: A liger (lion father, tiger mother) grows much larger than either parent species, whereas a tigon (tiger father, lion mother) does not. Both hybrids receive one set of lion chromosomes and one set of tiger chromosomes. What is the epigenetic explanation for the difference?
options: The two hybrids inherit different combinations of lion and tiger alleles for the genes controlling growth
Some tags on growth genes survive in the sperm and ovum, so a gene's expression depends on its parent of origin
All epigenetic tags are removed from the gametes, so the difference must come from the uterus
Tags acquired by the body cells of the lion father during his life were passed to the liger
mcqs.specStatementText: Most tags are wiped from gametes, but not all: ligers and tigons
mcqs.explain: Most but not all epigenetic tags are removed from the gametes. Tags that remain on growth-related genes differ between lion and tiger sperm and ova, so the same genes are expressed differently in the liger and the tigon.
rationales: A student who expects every inherited difference to be genetic picks this. The stem states that both hybrids receive one lion set and one tiger set; the alleles are the same combination, supplied by different parents.

Most but not all epigenetic tags are removed from the gametes. Tags that remain on growth-related genes differ between lion and tiger sperm and ova, so the same genes are expressed differently in the liger and the tigon.

A student who thinks the gametes are wiped clean picks this. If every tag were removed, the reciprocal hybrids would carry the same tags; it is the tags that are not removed that make parent of origin matter.
A student who thinks acquired changes in body cells reach offspring picks this. The tags that matter are those present in the sperm and ovum; tags in a parent's somatic cells are not transmitted.

mcqs.q: In a study, the DNA methylation patterns of pairs of monozygotic twins were compared. Three-year-old twins had almost identical patterns. Fifty-year-old twins showed large differences, and the differences were greatest in pairs who had spent the most years living apart. What is the best interpretation?
options: The methylation differences show that the older twins' DNA base sequences had changed
The older pairs cannot have been monozygotic, because identical twins are alike in every respect
Differences in the twins' environments over time altered their patterns of gene expression
The older twins who lived together must have differed genetically, since their environments were the same
mcqs.specStatementText: Identical twins reveal environmental effects on expression
mcqs.explain: Monozygotic twins share a genome, so differences in methylation cannot be genetic. The growth of the differences with age, and especially with time apart, shows the environment acting on gene expression through epigenetic tags.
rationales: A student who treats methylation as a mutation picks this. Methyl tags alter gene expression without altering the base sequence, so the twins remain genetically identical.

A student who takes 'identical' to cover gene activity as well as genome picks this. Monozygotic twins have the same DNA but can develop different epigenetic tags, which is exactly what makes them useful for this kind of study.

Monozygotic twins share a genome, so differences in methylation cannot be genetic. The growth of the differences with age, and especially with time apart, shows the environment acting on gene expression through epigenetic tags.
A student who equates environment with the home picks this. Twins living together still differ in diet, illness, habits and exposures, and monozygotic twins do not differ genetically.

mcqs.q: Estrogen is a steroid hormone that passes through the plasma membrane of its target cells. How does estrogen alter the pattern of gene expression in these cells?
options: It binds to a receptor protein, and the hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor
It binds directly to the promoters of its target genes in place of a transcription factor
It activates enzymes already in the cell by binding to their active sites, without any transcription
It adds methyl tags to cytosine in the promoters of target genes, switching them on
mcqs.specStatementText: A hormone and a nutrient can change gene expression
mcqs.explain: Estrogen binds to a receptor inside the cell; the complex binds to specific base sequences in DNA and alters transcription of target genes. The hormone therefore acts through a protein that binds DNA, as all regulation of transcription does.
rationales: Estrogen binds to a receptor inside the cell; the complex binds to specific base sequences in DNA and alters transcription of target genes. The hormone therefore acts through a protein that binds DNA, as all regulation of transcription does.
A student who leaves out the receptor picks this. Regulation of transcription is by proteins binding to DNA; estrogen has to bind to a receptor protein, and it is the complex that binds the DNA.

A student who reaches for enzyme activation picks this. Estrogen's effect on the pattern of gene expression is a change in which genes are transcribed, so new proteins are made rather than existing enzymes activated.

A student who thinks a methyl tag marks a gene for use picks this. Promoter methylation represses transcription, and the hormone acts through a receptor that becomes a transcription factor, not by methylating DNA.

mcqs.q: Why is it important that most epigenetic tags are removed from the DNA of the sperm and the ovum?
options: So that no epigenetic tag from either parent is able to affect the offspring's cells
So that the cells of the embryo can develop a fresh pattern of differentiation
So that the base sequence of the offspring's DNA is restored to normal
So that every gene in the zygote is switched off until it is needed
mcqs.specStatementText: Most tags are wiped from gametes, but not all: ligers and tigons
mcqs.explain: Removing most of the tags from the gametes means the embryo is not committed to the expression patterns of the parents' cells, so its cells can differentiate into every cell type. The tags that are not removed are the exception that makes ligers and tigons differ.
rationales: A student who thinks the gametes are wiped completely clean picks this. Most but not all tags are removed; some remain, and these affect how certain genes are expressed according to the parent that supplied them.

Removing most of the tags from the gametes means the embryo is not committed to the expression patterns of the parents' cells, so its cells can differentiate into every cell type. The tags that are not removed are the exception that makes ligers and tigons differ.

A student who thinks tags alter the sequence picks this. Epigenetic tags do not change the base sequence, so there is nothing in the sequence to restore; removing tags changes only the pattern of expression.

A student who takes tags to be 'on' labels picks this. Many tags, such as promoter methylation, repress genes, so removing them does not switch every gene off; it resets the pattern so that a new one can be established.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D2.2 Gene expression

specStatements.text: How a gene reaches the phenotype: transcription, translation, protein at work
Proteins bind promoters and enhancers to control transcription
How long an mRNA lasts controls how much protein is made
Cells differentiate by expressing different genes, not by changing DNA
Genome, transcriptome and proteome are not the same list
Methyl tags on promoters and histones
Expression patterns can be inherited if tags stay in place
The environment changes which genes are expressed

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Histone methylation is treated only at the level the guidance sets: methyl groups added to amino acids in histones can cause transcription to be repressed or activated. No object names the specific amino acid residues or positions involved, the enzymes that add or remove the tags, the proteins that read them, or how the tags alter chromatin packing or the access of RNA polymerase.

Epigenetic inheritance is tested only as the possibility that a pattern of gene expression is passed to daughter cells or offspring because tags remain in place through mitosis or meiosis. No item asks how methylation patterns are copied during DNA replication, and no transgenerational human cohort study is used as evidence.

Monozygotic twin studies appear only as a way of investigating how the environment affects gene expression in genetically identical people. No object compares monozygotic with dizygotic twins, calculates concordance rates or heritability, or uses twins to estimate the genetic contribution to a trait.

Exactly one hormone (estrogen) and one biochemical (lactose acting on the lac operon of Escherichia coli) are used. Tryptophan and the trp operon are not included, no other hormone is used as an example, and the additional control of the lac operon by glucose (catabolite repression, cAMP and CAP) is left out.
